questions.stem: You are examining the feet of Patrick, 63, who has type 2 diabetes and 6 months of numbness in both feet. Shoes and socks are off and there is mild callus under both first metatarsal heads. You are about to test protective sensation with a 10 g monofilament. Which technique is correct?
options: Drag it along the sole from heel to toe and ask when he first feels it
Press it on the callus under the first metatarsal head, where ulcers most often form
Press perpendicular until it buckles for about 2 s, eyes closed, avoiding callus
Press it until the skin blanches, with his eyes open so he can watch each touch
questions.why: The monofilament is pressed at right angles to the skin until it bends (which delivers 10 g) for about 2 seconds, with the patient's eyes closed, at the plantar forefoot sites and hallux. Avoid callus, scar and ulcers, because thick skin can make sensation seem absent when it is not.
notes: Dragging tests light touch moving across the skin, not a fixed 10 g pressure, so it does not assess protective sensation.
Callus dulls sensation and gives a false absent response, so test next to it, never on it.
>10 g and blanching are not the end point, and with his eyes open he can see when he is touched, which defeats the test.

questions.stem: Patrick, 63, has type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 8.9% (74 mmol/mol) and eGFR 72. He admits he rarely takes his immediate-release metformin because it gives him diarrhoea. He has never tried any other formulation or strategy. What is the most appropriate change to his glucose-lowering treatment now?
options: Stop metformin and start an SGLT2 inhibitor such as empagliflozin on its own
Change to metformin XR 500 mg once daily with the evening meal, titrating slowly
Stop metformin and start gliclazide MR 30 mg once daily with breakfast
Start insulin glargine 10 units at night and keep metformin for when he can manage
questions.why: Metformin is first line, and gut intolerance is often managed by taking it with food, starting low and titrating slowly, or switching to the extended-release form. Try this before giving up on it. Add a second agent (an SGLT2 inhibitor is favoured if the albuminuria is confirmed) if HbA1c is still above target at 3 months.
notes: Stopping metformin is premature because he has not tried the measures that usually make it tolerable. An SGLT2 inhibitor is normally added to metformin, not used instead of it.
A sulfonylurea risks hypoglycaemia and weight gain, which is a bad choice in a man who is already unsteady and at risk of falls, and metformin has not yet failed.
Insulin is not needed for an asymptomatic HbA1c of 8.9% when oral treatment has never been taken properly.

questions.stem: Patrick, 63, has diabetic peripheral neuropathy and feels unsteady in the dark. He stands steadily with his feet together and eyes open, but sways and nearly falls when he closes his eyes. He has no postural drop and his power is near normal. What is the mechanism of this positive Romberg test?
options: Loss of joint position input from large myelinated sensory fibres, made up for by vision
Cerebellar vermis dysfunction that impairs coordination of the trunk muscles during stance
Postural hypotension from autonomic neuropathy that reduces cerebral perfusion on standing
Weakness of the ankle dorsiflexors from loss of distal motor axons
questions.why: Balance depends on vision, vestibular input and proprioception. When large-fibre neuropathy removes joint position sense from the feet, vision makes up for it, so balance fails only when the eyes close or it is dark. This is sensory ataxia.
notes: Cerebellar ataxia makes the patient unsteady even with the eyes open, so Romberg is not positive in the true sense.
He has no postural drop, and hypotension would not depend on whether his eyes are open or closed.
Motor weakness causes the same unsteadiness whether or not he can see, and his power is near normal.

questions.stem: Examining Patrick, 63, who has diabetic peripheral neuropathy, you find both ankle reflexes absent even with reinforcement, while both knee reflexes are present. Losing the ankle jerk first fits a length-dependent neuropathy. Which spinal root and peripheral nerve carry the ankle reflex arc?
options: L3 and L4 roots via the femoral nerve
L5 root via the common fibular nerve
S2 to S4 roots via the pudendal nerve
S1 root via the tibial nerve
questions.why: The ankle jerk is an S1 reflex carried in the sciatic nerve and then its tibial branch to gastrocnemius and soleus. It is the longest reflex arc in the body, so it is lost before the knee jerk (L3 to L4, femoral nerve) in a length-dependent neuropathy.
notes: L3 and L4 through the femoral nerve carry the knee jerk, which is preserved here.
The common fibular nerve supplies the anterior and lateral leg compartments. L5 has no reliable routine reflex and does not carry the ankle jerk.
S2 to S4 through the pudendal nerve serve the anal and bulbocavernosus reflexes and saddle sensation, not the ankle jerk.
